title: Human Immunodeficiency Virus Infection
subject: Medicine
summary: HIV infection is a chronic retroviral disease causing progressive CD4+ T‑cell loss and immune failure. Staging follows WHO clinical stages and CD4 counts. Management combines antiretroviral therapy, opportunistic infection prophylaxis and supportive care, adapted to low‑resource settings.

sections.p: HIV is a lentivirus that infects CD4+ T‑lymphocytes, macrophages and dendritic cells, leading to gradual immune collapse. Diagnosis requires detection of viral antigen or nucleic acid, or serology after the window period.
b: Positive rapid HIV‑1/2 antibody test or 4th‑generation Ag/Ab combo.
Confirmatory HIV‑1 RNA PCR if initial test is discordant.
Baseline CD4 count and full blood count to assess immune status.

sections.p: Two systems are used: WHO clinical stages (1‑4) based on symptoms, and CD4 count thresholds. Staging guides prophylaxis and urgency of ART initiation.
b: Stage 1: Asymptomatic, CD4 ≥ 500 cells/µL.
Stage 2: Mild opportunistic infections, CD4 350‑499 cells/µL.
Stage 3: Advanced infections, CD4 200‑349 cells/µL.
Stage 4 (AIDS): Severe disease, CD4 < 200 cells/µL or AIDS‑defining illness.

sections.p: HIV infection is acquired through blood, sexual contact, or mother‑to‑child transmission. In East Africa, heterosexual transmission and perinatal spread dominate.
b: Unprotected vaginal intercourse (most common).
Mother‑to‑child transmission during pregnancy, delivery or breastfeeding.
Unsafe medical injections or blood transfusion.
Intravenous drug use (less common locally).

sections.p: Early infection may be asymptomatic or present with a self‑limited febrile illness (acute retroviral syndrome). Chronic infection progresses to weight loss, chronic diarrhoea, oral candidiasis, and opportunistic infections.
b: Acute phase: fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, sore throat (2‑4 weeks post‑exposure).
Chronic phase: persistent fever, night sweats, weight loss, lymphadenopathy.
AIDS‑defining illnesses: TB, cryptococcal meningitis, Kaposi sarcoma, PCP.

sections.p: Testing must answer three questions: presence of infection, immune status, and co‑morbidities.

t.b: Is the patient infected? Positive result confirms infection; negative requires repeat after window period.
How active is replication? Detectable > 1000 copies/mL indicates uncontrolled infection; guides ART monitoring.
What is immune competence? < 200 cells/µL defines AIDS; thresholds guide prophylaxis.

t.a: Full blood count and liver function tests
t.b: Baseline organ status before ART; anemia or transaminitis may affect drug choice.

t.a: Screen for TB (sputum GeneXpert or chest X‑ray)
t.b: Is co‑existent TB present? Positive test mandates TB treatment before or with ART.

t.a: If PCR unavailable: repeat rapid test after 4 weeks
t.b: Confirm infection when molecular testing not possible; ensures false‑negative window is covered.

sections.p: Rapid CD4 decline, opportunistic infections, and HIV‑associated malignancies signal imminent deterioration.
b: CD4 < 50 cells/µL with fever → consider disseminated TB or cryptococcal meningitis.
Persistent diarrhoea > 2 weeks → think CMV colitis.
New skin lesions → rule out Kaposi sarcoma or bacillary angiomatosis.

sections.p: Start lifelong combination antiretroviral therapy (cART) as soon as diagnosis is confirmed, regardless of CD4 count, unless contraindicated.
b: First‑line regimen (low‑resource WHO recommendation): Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Efavirenz.
Avoid protease inhibitors in severe liver disease; avoid efavirenz in pregnancy after first trimester.
Provide cotrimoxazole prophylaxis when CD4 < 350 cells/µL or WHO stage ≥ 2.
Treat active TB before ART if CD4 < 50 cells/µL; otherwise start ART within 2 weeks of TB therapy.
Manage opportunistic infections with guideline‑directed regimens (e.g., fluconazole for cryptococcal meningitis).

sections.p: Regular monitoring of viral load and CD4 count assesses treatment success. Prevention includes counseling, condom distribution, PMTCT, and needle‑safety.
b: Viral load at 3 months, then every 6 months; aim for < 50 copies/mL.
CD4 count every 6‑12 months; increase indicates immune recovery.
PMTCT: maternal ART from 14 weeks gestation, infant prophylaxis with nevirapine for 6 weeks.
Community education on safe sex and safe injection practices.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic HIV‑related weight loss and lymphadenopathy.
b: Tuberculosis – chronic cough, night sweats; differentiate with sputum GeneXpert.
Malaria – intermittent fever, splenomegaly; malaria rapid test helps.
Lymphoma – rapidly enlarging nodes; biopsy required.

sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely normal early in infection or altered by co‑morbidities.
b: Rapid antibody test may be negative during the window period; repeat after 4 weeks.
CD4 count can be transiently elevated during acute infections; interpret trends.
Liver enzymes may rise from ART rather than hepatitis; review medication history.

whenToSeekHelp: New neurological deficits or severe headache

faq.a: No; current therapy suppresses replication but does not eradicate latent reservoirs.

faq.q: Why start ART regardless of CD4 count?
faq.a: Early treatment reduces morbidity, transmission risk and improves survival.

faq.q: What is the most common opportunistic infection in East Africa?
faq.a: Pulmonary tuberculosis, often presenting with chronic cough and weight loss.

exam: What immediate investigations would you order for a newly diagnosed HIV patient presenting with fever and cough? — Rapid HIV test confirmation, CD4 count, sputum GeneXpert, full blood count, liver function; to identify TB and immune status.

A patient on first‑line cART develops new skin lesions and lymphadenopathy. How do you differentiate Kaposi sarcoma from bacillary angiomatosis? — Look for violaceous plaques, HHV‑8 serology, and response to azithromycin; biopsy if uncertain.
Why is efavirenz avoided in the first trimester of pregnancy? — It is teratogenic, associated with neural tube defects; alternative regimens use nevirapine or integrase inhibitors.

Explain the rationale for giving cotrimoxazole prophylaxis in a patient with CD4 = 300 cells/µL. — Prevents Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and bacterial infections; WHO recommends at WHO stage ≥ 2 or CD4 < 350 cells/µL.

A patient with HIV and CD4 = 45 cells/µL presents with headache and neck stiffness. What is your next step? — Perform lumbar puncture for cryptococcal antigen; start high‑dose fluconazole while arranging amphotericin if available.
How does TB co‑infection alter the timing of ART initiation? — Start TB treatment first; if CD4 < 50 cells/µL begin ART within 2 weeks, otherwise within 8 weeks to reduce IRIS risk.
What are the WHO clinical stage criteria for stage 3 disease? — Unexplained severe weight loss, chronic diarrhoea, persistent fever, oral candidiasis, pulmonary TB, severe bacterial infections.

Describe how you would counsel a serodiscordant couple on prevention of HIV transmission. — Emphasize consistent condom use, ART for the positive partner to achieve viral suppression, and consider pre‑exposure prophylaxis for the negative partner.
